name: PT Eagle High Plantations Tbk

frontmatter.title: Eagle High Plantations — a levered estate priced for refinancing, not for a palm collapse
frontmatter.summary: Eagle High earns 28.5% EBITDA margins, with nine-month filings putting unit cash cost at Rp12,950,000 a tonne and IDR1,908.1bn of FY2026E EBITDA. Equity is a stub under IDR4,882.7bn of gross debt; at Rp78 the reverse DCF implies CPO of US$1,157/t, barely below spot, so the discount is refinancing, not a palm collapse. BUY at Rp303 (291.6%) [S0, S5, S6, S7].
thesis: The reverse DCF says the price discounts CPO of US$1,157/t in FY2027E, against a deck spot of 1,180.0 USD/t and a forward strip of 1,240.0 USD/t. That is a flat-to-soft palm price, not a trough: the 2023-24 realised band was far lower, so the market is not pricing a commodity collapse [S0].

Unit economics are re-anchored on the filing, not on FY2025: nine-month cost of sales took a larger share of revenue, and the implied unit cash cost is Rp12,950,000 a tonne. FY2026E EBITDA is IDR1,908.1bn, below the last audited year in margin terms, and the cost escalates into the terminal [S7, S5].

Leverage is the story: gross debt of IDR4,882.7bn against cash of IDR120.8bn and a market capitalisation of IDR2,427.5bn means the equity is a call on the estate, and the current portion of borrowings plus the rolling short bonds make refinancing, not palm oil, the first-order risk [S7, S0].

The capital structure is being repaired but not deleveraged: a quasi-reorganisation cleared the accumulated deficit against share premium, and the first dividend was declared on 30 October 2026 — IDR31.1bn, 8.6% of first-half attributable profit [S4, S7].

The scenario ladder is mirrored on price, volume, cost and the cost of capital. Purchased FFB and CPO are most of cost of sales and are priced off CPO, so cost now rises with the bull price and falls with the bear; the bear case is an equity wipeout on the primary DCF, and the bull needs CPO only a fifth above the deck [S7, S6].

catalysts.event: Interim dividend of one rupiah a share paid; the first distribution after the quasi-reorganisation
FY2026 audited results, the final dividend decision and the full-year unit-cost print
January-February 2027 FFB intake, the El Nino effect on yields and the March A-series bond maturity
Kernel crushing plant commissioning and first PKO/PKM revenue
B50 biodiesel mandate implementation, the main swing factor for domestic CPO demand

blocks.text: **BUY, target Rp303.** PT Eagle High Plantations is a mid-sized Indonesian oil-palm grower and miller with 87,000 ha hectares planted across Kalimantan, Sumatra and Papua, plus a mill extension in East Kalimantan completed in 2025 [S6]. At 30 September 2026 it carried IDR4,882.7bn of gross borrowings and IDR120.8bn of cash against a market capitalisation of IDR2,427.5bn [S7, S0]. Leverage is why the equity is simultaneously cheap on cash flow and dangerous on refinancing.

The price is Rp78 on 6 November 2026 [S0]. Our target is Rp303, a total return of 291.6% including the declared interim dividend. It is a probability-weighted blend of a through-cycle DCF at 11.4% WACC (60%), an EV/EBITDA cross-check (25%) and price-to-book (15%), with the declared interim carried as a negative bridge item. The DCF value is Rp378; the base-scenario target before probability weighting is Rp350; the weighted target is Rp303.

**What the market is paying for.** At Rp78 the reverse DCF solves for a CPO price of US$1,157/t in FY2027E, only about three per cent below the deck spot of 1,180.0 USD/t and below the forward strip of 1,240.0 USD/t [S0]. That is not a trough expectation. The realised FY2023A and FY2024A prints were 886.0 USD/t and 963.0 USD/t, and today's implied price is well above both. The equity is cheap because the market applies a refinancing discount to a thin, levered stub, not because it forecasts a palm collapse. Stating it the other way round was the draft's error and it is corrected here.

**Why this is not the most cautious view, and not the most hopeful one.** Unit cash cost is set at Rp12,950,000 a tonne, the rate the filed nine-month cost of sales ratio implies, not the lower FY2025 rate [S7, S5]. Part of it escalates with the rupiah CPO path, because purchased fruit and traded CPO are most of the cost base, so the correction compounds into the terminal value. Realisation is held at 0.96, just below the nine-month actual, a small haircut for the purchased-volume mix. The tax rate is 35.0% against a FY2025 effective charge above fifty per cent, so the charge is normalised down, not up. We have added no volume decline and no grade haircut. The base case is the most probable path: the filed cost, the company's mill capacity and the deck's price.

**What moves the value.** The three load-bearing assumptions are the CPO deck, the volume path from the mill extension and purchased intake, and unit cash cost; each is tested in section four. The largest risk is not palm oil: it is refinancing. The current portion of borrowings and debt-like liabilities exceeds cash, the short A-series bonds roll annually, and a 11.4% WACC assumes the rupiah debt market stays open to a company that has just cleared its deficit [S5, S7].

Eagle High is an upstream palm business: it grows oil palm, harvests fresh fruit bunches, mills them into crude palm oil and palm kernel, and sells all three. There is no refining of consequence yet. It reports two segments, plantations and manufacturing, but the economics are one spread — the CPO and kernel price against the cost of a tonne of fruit and the cost of milling it [S6].

The footprint is three islands. Plantations sit in Kalimantan, Sumatra and Papua and the group had 87,000 ha hectares planted at the end of 2025, including nucleus and plasma; that hectare figure is total planted area, not an undeveloped land bank, and no separate land-bank figure is disclosed [S6]. In the last audited year the company produced 286,972 t of CPO, 55,470 t of palm kernel and 1,085,692 t of FFB, at an oil extraction rate of 23.3% [S6].

Two features matter for valuation. First, sales exceed production: CPO sales were 358 kt against production of 286,972 t, because the company buys third-party FFB and trades CPO alongside its own crop [S6]. Purchased volumes carry a thinner margin, which is why the blended realisation is not the own-crop ratio. Second, the mills are underutilised: processing roughly one and a quarter million tonnes of FFB through the installed capacity implies utilisation in the mid-forties per cent, so the constraint on growth is fruit supply and working capital, not milling [S6].

Strategy is self-funded and incremental. The East Kalimantan mill extension was completed in 2025 and 2026 capital is allocated to a kernel crushing plant that turns kernel into palm kernel oil and meal, a first downstream step [S6]. Capex was IDR338.2bn in the last audited year, roughly a fifth of EBITDA, and the nine-month 2026 cash flow shows a similar run-rate [S5, S0]. No land expansion is announced; growth comes from yield, intake and the derivative line.

Ownership is concentrated. Insiders hold 77.3% and the public float is 24.0% [S0]. The pack also reports institutions at 2.2%, but that category overlaps the float rather than adding to it, so the register does not sum to a hundred and the categories must not be added. The controlling shareholder is the Rajawali group; the register has been stable through the quasi-reorganisation and no rights issue is announced, so the share count of 31,122.4 million is held flat [S0]. The company is a challenger: a small share of national CPO output against the Astra, Salim and Sinar Mas estates. Its edge is geographic spread across three islands; its disadvantage is scale and a balance sheet with less room to absorb a trough.

Palm oil is globally priced and Indonesia is the largest producer. The deck has CPO averaging 1,135.0 USD/t this year, rising to 1,240.0 USD/t next year on the El Nino deficit and the biodiesel bid, then gliding to a long-run 1,150.0 USD/t [S0]. The near-term curve is supported by a backwardated Malaysian forward strip and the expectation that the 2026-27 El Nino hits 2027 FFB yields [S6].

Demand has a structural bid. Indonesia moved to a forty per cent biodiesel blend in 2025, absorbing around fourteen million tonnes of CPO equivalent, with a step to forty-five and then fifty per cent planned for 2026-27 [S6]. That raises domestic consumption and reduces the exportable surplus. The counterweight is the export levy and duty, which resets monthly with the reference price and is borne by the exporter; the annual report treats it as a wedge on realisations rather than a cost line, which is why we model no revenue royalty [S6, S5].

Supply is slow to respond. New planting is constrained by permits and sustainability rules, and Indonesia's replanting programme has run behind target; the annual report cites both as supports for prices [S6]. Malaysian output is constrained by tree age and labour. The marginal tonne is expensive to bring on, so price can stay above marginal cash cost for extended periods — a favourable structure for a high-cost, levered producer, whose risk is not collapse to cost but oscillation around a thin margin.

Competitive position is second quartile on cost with a levered balance sheet. Unit cash cost of about Rp12,950,000 a tonne of CPO sold is above the best Indonesian producers, which run in the high single-digit millions of rupiah, because the company buys a material share of its fruit and because Kalimantan and Papua haulage is expensive [S5, S7]. It does not need to be a cost leader: at the deck price the spread covers interest several times.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate — purchased FFB is priced off CPO, so the supplier captures part of any rise. Buyer power is low on a globally traded commodity. New entrants are constrained by land and permits. Substitutes such as soyoil and rapeseed matter at the margin and sit in the deck. Rivalry is global and price-based [S6, S5]. The moat is the planted estate: 87,000 ha of mature palms in a country where new planting is close to impossible to permit, currently priced below replacement cost.

The external influences that matter are the rupiah, the levy and the weather. Revenue is rupiah but priced off a dollar benchmark, so a weaker rupiah raises the rupiah price received; the deck has the rate at 17,570 rupiah to the dollar in FY2026E [S0]. The levy resets monthly. And the El Nino that supports 2027 prices is the same weather that suppresses this estate's yields — the company flagged above-average rainfall as a constraint in 2025 [S6].

Revenue in the last audited year was IDR5,761.3bn, up by a third, on higher volumes and a CPO price averaging Rp14,113/kg per kilogram [S6]. CPO was the overwhelming majority, kernel a smaller slice and FFB sales a rounding error; the annual report splits the three and shows volume growth in CPO and kernel [S6].

Margins widened with the price. Restated EBITDA was IDR1,644.7bn, a margin of 28.5%, and net profit attributable was IDR361.7bn or Rp12 per share [S5]. The critical correction to the data pack is depreciation: the pack reports only a fraction of the real charge, while the audited accounts carry IDR455.0bn through cost of goods sold [S5]. Without the restatement EBITDA is understated by roughly a quarter and every multiple is wrong; history in this report is restated from the filing, and the engine shows the restatement. The same defect runs through the pack's quarterly D&A and therefore its LTM EBITDA, which is why the cross-check in section four uses the restated last audited year rather than the pack's LTM; the datapack is not ours to edit and the defect is named for the Director.

The current year is re-anchored on the nine-month filing. Net sales were IDR5,386.9bn and cost of sales IDR4,007.8bn, leaving operating income of IDR1,015.5bn before D&A of IDR230.8bn of mature-plantation amortisation plus IDR118.4bn of depreciation [S7]. Applying our FY2026E revenue build of IDR7,466.3bn at the filed cost ratio gives EBITDA of IDR1,908.1bn, a 25.6% margin, against 28.5% in the last audited year. That is the number a Q4-seasonality build supports; the draft's higher figure required a margin step-change the filing does not contain.

The unit cost line is therefore the filing, not the FY2025 actual: we model Rp12,950,000 a tonne this year, escalating with the rupiah cost base, and carry SG&A at 6.8% of revenue, between the last audited year and the nine-month run-rate [S5, S7]. The engine's calibration gate compares FY2026E at FY2025 prices and volume with the FY2025 actual and flags a gap; we accept it, because the cost base moved with the 2026 price as purchased FFB and CPO are most of cost of sales. The justification is in the model.

Cash flow is the strongest part of the story. Operating cash flow covered capex of IDR338.2bn with room to spare, and free cash flow was positive after interest [S7, S5]. The nine-month 2026 cash flow shows capex of a similar scale and operating cash covering it [S7].

The balance sheet is the constraint. At 30 September 2026 gross debt was IDR4,882.7bn against IDR120.8bn of cash, so net debt was close to gross [S7]. That is high for a commodity producer and more levered than the forecast year-end position the model projects; the interest bill of IDR407.2bn is covered comfortably by EBITDA at the deck price. Maturities are not one wall but a rolling cycle: short-term bank and non-bank loans, leases, the short A-series bonds and the sukuk sit in current liabilities, and the nine-month cash flow shows bonds and sukuk being issued as older tranches are repaid [S7]. The refinancing dependency is real and is the first risk in section five.

Capital allocation has been conservative on dividends and aggressive on the balance sheet. No dividend was paid in the last four audited years because of the accumulated deficit [S0, S5]. The quasi-reorganisation cleared it against share premium and the board declared an interim of Rp1 a share, IDR31.1bn in total, equal to 8.6% of first-half attributable profit [S4]. We model a 10.0% payout thereafter, above the interim ratio and still leaving the rest for debt reduction.

Earnings quality: accruals are clean. Profit and operating cash flow track closely in every audited year, working capital is small because CPO sells on short cash terms, and there is no receivable build [S0]. Three flags are recorded. The first is the depreciation understatement in the pack, corrected from the filing. The second is the effective tax rate: the FY2025 charge was more than half of pre-tax profit because of non-deductible items [S5]; we model 35.0%, and a normalisation of the charge is upside not in our numbers. The third is the refinancing cycle itself, which shows as high current liabilities and repeated bond issuance rather than as an earnings item [S7].

Plantations are valued on through-cycle NAV, not spot earnings. The house method for commodity producers is a life-of-asset DCF at a sourced through-cycle price, less net debt, with P&L multiples as cross-checks rather than anchors. Here the primary is a ten-year FCFF DCF on the deck's CPO path with the terminal price escalating with the rupiah cost base, weighted at sixty per cent, with EV/EBITDA at a quarter and price-to-book at fifteen per cent.

The cost of capital is high because the equity is levered. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature premium plus country risk gives a cost of equity of 19.5% on a levered beta of 2.05, and the debt weight is two thirds at a pre-tax cost of 9.4%, giving a WACC of 11.4% [S0]. That is the right shape for a company whose enterprise value is mostly debt: the equity is a call option on the palm price and should be discounted at an equity rate that reflects it.

The DCF produces Rp378 per share on the base case, with 50.8% of the value in the terminal. The base-scenario target before probability weighting is Rp350 and the probability-weighted target is Rp303. The earlier draft attributed the blend to the DCF; the DCF and the blend are different numbers and are now shown separately.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check is struck on a restated basis. The metric is the restated last audited year, IDR1,644.7bn, not the data pack's LTM of a corrupted series: the pack's quarterly D&A is a small fraction of the filed charge, so its LTM EBITDA is understated and unusable [S5, S7]. We use the peer median multiple of 6.1 because the company's own five-year multiple series is computed from the same corrupted EBITDA — the pack's own-history multiple is materially higher than the same year restated from the filing — so blending it in would flatter the cross-check rather than discipline it [S0, S5]. The result is Rp176.

The P/BV cross-check uses the peer median of 1.6 on filed equity, giving Rp158. Book is carried at historical cost for land acquired years ago and understates the estate, which is part of why this cross-check sits far below the DCF. The divergence is not a trough-year artefact, as the draft claimed: it is the difference between a ten-year cash-flow model and two static single-year metrics, and both are flagged by the engine. We keep the config weights and explain the divergence rather than bending the method. The bridge uses the data pack's cash balance rather than the filed cash at 30 September 2026 [S7, S0]; the difference is immaterial at the share level and does not affect the rating, and the filed figure is the one used in the balance-sheet discussion in section three.

The sensitivity that matters is the mirrored ladder in section five, not a two-way grid. We withdraw the engine's price-by-FX surface: its shock routine rewrites the deck's long-run CPO values on every run, so its central cell does not reconcile with the headline DCF, and it gives different answers for equivalent price and FX moves although revenue is CPO times the rupiah rate. An exhibit that contradicts the base and misstates its own slope should not be printed, and the earlier claim that a one-tenth CPO move is worth more than the market capitalisation was false on the withdrawn grid and is retracted. Read the ladder instead: the base blended value is Rp350, the bear Rp80 and the bull Rp521, and the reverse DCF below is solved on the same model that produces the headline DCF of Rp378.

What the price implies is the most useful number here. The reverse DCF solves for the CPO price that equates the DCF to the market price: US$1,157/t in the reference year, against a deck of 1,240.0 USD/t and a spot of 1,180.0 USD/t [S0]. The market is pricing a palm price at or just below spot, sustained, on a levered estate. It is not pricing the 2023-24 band. The gap between our value and the price is therefore a refinancing and discount-rate gap, not a commodity disagreement: either the market assigns a materially higher probability to a liquidity event than our WACC implies, or the equity is mispriced. We say the latter, with the caveat that the price can stay wrong longer than a levered company can stay solvent — which is why the balance sheet, not the palm price, is the real risk.

The dividend-capacity cross-check supports the same conclusion. At the model's through-cycle free cash flow to equity and a 10.0% payout, the FCFE yield is 38.7% at FY2026E and 47.1% at FY2027E. The company could pay far more, or retire debt; the model retains cash and does not distribute it. A re-rating path therefore exists through a higher payout or faster deleveraging, and the bull scenario assumes the latter. The declared interim is Rp1 a share [S4]; this is a deleveraging story with a token distribution, not an income stock.

**Post-balance-sheet review.** We searched the company site and press since 30 September 2026. The capital events are the interim dividend declared on 30 October 2026 [S4], the quasi-reorganisation that cleared the accumulated deficit against share premium without changing total equity [S7], and the continuing refinancing cycle in the nine-month cash flow, with bonds and sukuk issued and bank facilities rolled [S7]. The short A-series bonds mature in January and March 2027 and the B-series in 2028, 2029 and 2031 [S7]. No divestment, rights issue or acquisition is disclosed. The kernel crushing plant is the only committed development project and has no disclosed budget; it is carried at IDR297.3bn of nine-month property, plant and equipment spend as a conservative sunk-cost proxy, because the model does not yet earn its revenue.
Risks are ranked by what they would do to the equity, not by how often they are discussed.

**Refinancing and liquidity — high likelihood, severe impact.** Gross debt of IDR4,882.7bn against cash of IDR120.8bn and a market capitalisation of IDR2,427.5bn means the debt is worth more than the equity. The current portion of borrowings and debt-like liabilities — bank, non-bank, leases, the short bonds and the sukuk — comes due inside twelve months and exceeds the cash balance [S7]. The bonds are a rolling programme: the short A-series tranches mature in January and March 2027 and are refinanced, while the B-series run to 2028, 2029 and 2031 [S7]. A refinancing at a wider spread, a covenant breach on an EBITDA fall or a dividend cut to protect liquidity transfers value to lenders quickly. The stale claim that the bond runs through the end of the decade is withdrawn. This is the risk that would change our rating.

**CPO price — medium likelihood, severe impact.** The reverse DCF shows how much value is price. A fall to the 2023-24 realised average takes the equity toward the bear case; the mitigant is the biodiesel bid and constrained supply [S6].

**Unit cost — high likelihood, moderate impact.** The nine-month accounts already show the cost ratio deteriorating. If purchased-FFB costs keep rising faster than CPO, the margin per tonne compresses even at a flat price. We have built in the deterioration; the risk is that it is worse than the nine-month run-rate [S7].

**Weather and yield — medium likelihood, moderate impact.** The El Nino that supports prices suppresses this estate's own yields, especially in Kalimantan and Papua; above-average rainfall was already a constraint in 2025 [S6].

**Governance and control — medium likelihood, moderate impact.** A controller with roughly three quarters of the register and a float of 24.0% leaves minorities little influence over related-party flows or capital allocation [S0]. The quasi-reorganisation was value-neutral in total equity but resets distributable reserves, and the dividend policy is new.

**Currency — low likelihood, moderate impact.** A stronger rupiah would cut the rupiah value of dollar-priced CPO while costs stay in rupiah; the deck has the FY2026E rate at 17,570 rupiah to the dollar [S0].
**Regulatory — low likelihood, moderate impact.** Export levy changes and the biodiesel mandate are the two levers: a levy rise compresses realisations, a faster move to B50 supports prices [S6].

The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers, and the cost shock follows the price. Purchased FFB and CPO were most of nine-month cost of sales and are priced off CPO [S7]; with about two thirds of the cost base purchased, a one-fifth CPO move passes through roughly thirteen per cent of cost. The bear therefore cuts unit cost with the price rather than raising it, and the bull raises cost with the price rather than cutting it; the draft had the mirror inverted and it is corrected. Probabilities are 30% bear, 50% base and 20% bull, reflecting a genuinely two-sided palm price and the refinancing likelihood.

The bear is a genuine distress branch. Price falls to four fifths of the deck, volume slips, purchased cost falls only partly because own-crop costs are sticky, and the refinancing spread widens by two percentage points; on the primary DCF the equity value floors at zero — a wipeout. The blended bear of Rp80 is higher than zero only because the two static cross-checks (a quarter and fifteen per cent of the weight) do not re-price a stress case; on the primary method the downside is total. The bull sets price a fifth above the deck, volume five per cent higher, purchased cost up with the price and the spread tighter; it is worth Rp521. The base is worth Rp350.

The price sits below even the blended bear case, so no probability mix inside this ladder makes the current price a fair bet. That is the arithmetic of a distressed equity: the market is pricing either a branch worse than our bear or a materially higher discount rate than our WACC. The reverse DCF reconciles the two readings — at spot-ish CPO the market's price implies a refinancing discount, not a commodity collapse. The probability that matters is therefore the probability of a liquidity event, and it is the number we monitor; the base case assumes the rolling refinancing succeeds because the nine-month cash flow shows it succeeding.

**Signposts that would change the view.** A covenant waiver, a refinancing at a wider spread or a dividend cut would move us to the bear regardless of the palm price. A sustained CPO print above the deck's next-year number with stable unit costs would move us to the bull. The first full quarter of kernel crushing output would reopen the volume path.

The controlling shareholder is the Rajawali group. Insiders hold 77.3% and the public 24.0% [S0]; the pack's institution figure overlaps the float, so the register categories do not sum to a hundred. The board is led by a president director who is also acting chief operating officer, with a finance director and operational and corporate directors [S0].

Two governance assertions in the draft were not evidenced and are downgraded. First, the archived FY2025 filing contains the contents entry for an independent auditors' report but not the opinion wording, so we cannot assert that the accounts were audited without qualification; the statement is unverified, not confirmed [S5]. Second, the absence of a special-monitoring-board designation or a notation letter cannot be established from company filings at all, and the archived news page we hold itself carries IDX headlines on the watch list, so we do not assert absence; the status is unchecked and should be confirmed against the exchange announcement before any position is sized [S4].

The governance event of the year was the quasi-reorganisation: the company cleared the accumulated deficit against share premium, restoring distributable reserves without changing total equity [S4, S7]. It is a legitimate mechanical step used by Indonesian companies emerging from losses, but it resets the accounting position, not the operating history. The dividend followed immediately, which suggests the exercise was done to enable distributions rather than to flatter the balance sheet.

Related-party exposure is small and quantified. Trade payables to affiliates were IDR11.5bn, 0.16% of total liabilities at 30 September 2026, and no related-party sales or purchases of fruit are disclosed in the note; the 2025 balance also carried IDR31.3bn of nine-month board remuneration, 13.4% of general and administrative expenses [S7 note 43]. The related parties are PT Rajawali Corpora and its affiliates, and the bank facilities are supported by a corporate guarantee from Rajawali Corpora, a benefit that also concentrates control [S7 note 43]. Plasma cooperatives sit outside the consolidated entity and the plasma receivable is the item to watch, because it is effectively financing to smallholders whose recoverability depends on scheme economics [S5].

ESG exposure is concentrated in certification and land. The company holds RSPO certification at several mills and ISPO across most operating units, covering the majority of planted area [S6]. That matters commercially: European buyers pay a premium for certified oil, and the annual report links certification to its export strategy. Some planted areas were acquired before the current permitting regime; titles are stated to be renewable, but Indonesian land disputes make this a tail risk rather than a base-case item [S5].

Dividend record: nothing in the four audited years to FY2025, then an interim of Rp1 a share declared on 30 October 2026 with record date 12 November 2026 [S4, S0]. The policy is new and the payout small against free cash flow, which leaves room for debt reduction or a step-up; the first is more likely given the leverage.

The near-term catalysts are dated [S4, S6, S7]. The interim dividend pays in late November 2026. The short A-series bonds mature in January and March 2027 and their replacement terms — price, tenor, covenant — are the single largest swing factor in the equity, because the whole valuation is a levered stub: a wider spread compresses the DCF directly and can trigger the distress branch [S7]. The FY2026 audited results in February 2027 will show whether the unit-cost reset is permanent or a one-year effect. First-quarter 2027 FFB intake will show the El Nino effect on yields. The kernel crushing plant, carried in the valuation bridge at the nine-month property, plant and equipment spend directed at it, should commission in the first half of 2027 and add a derivative revenue line the model does not yet earn from; commissioning is the trigger to move it from a sunk-cost proxy into the cash flow [S6, S7]. The B50 decision later in 2027 is the main swing factor for domestic demand.

The KPIs we watch are five [S5, S7]. First, unit cash cost per tonne of CPO sold, which is the thesis and the item the red team re-anchored: the bear case turns on it staying near the filed nine-month rate rather than reverting to the FY2025 number. Second, the ratio of purchased FFB and CPO to own crop, which sets how much of a CPO move passes through to margin and therefore whether the cost and price mirrors hold. Third, current borrowings against cash — at 30 September 2026 the current portion of borrowings and debt-like liabilities exceeds the cash balance, so any quarter that does not roll the short paper is a solvency question, not a valuation question. Fourth, net debt to EBITDA, which is the rating and the covenant. Fifth, CPO against the deck's next-year number, plus certification coverage as a slow-moving sixth. We will update on any of these and on any refinancing announcement; the valuation is levered enough that one quarter can move it materially, and the monitoring list is deliberately short. We would revisit the rating on a covenant event, a dividend cut or a sustained move in the palm price away from the deck.

S4.title: BWPT Bagikan Dividen Interim Rp31,12 Miliar Akhir November

bear.narrative: Refinancing stress meets a weaker palm: CPO falls back toward the 2023-24 realised band, the rolling A-series bonds and Rp1.06trn of debt-like current liabilities are refinanced at a wider spread, and the unit cost falls only partly with CPO because own-crop labour and fertiliser are sticky. Volume slips as mills run below intake and the dividend is cut to protect liquidity; the wider WACC captures the transfer of value to lenders.

bull.narrative: B50 biodiesel demand and a tight 2027 FFB supply keep CPO at the deck's 1240 forward strip through the forecast; purchased FFB and CPO cost rises with the CPO price rather than falling, so the margin gain is on own crop only. The kernel crushing plant adds PKO and PKM revenue, the East Kalimantan extension lifts intake, free cash flow cuts debt and the refinancing spread narrows.

assumptions.label: CPO sales volume (kt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 actual CPO sales 358.1 kt (S6 p.15). FY2026E 390 kt (+8.9% on 358.1 kt): nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp5,386.9bn is 28% above the same period of 2025 (S0) against a CPO benchmark up only about 13% (d.agri.cpo FY2025A 1007 to FY2026E 1135), so volumes, not only price, carried the growth; management guides higher CPO/PK/FFB production in 2026 (S6 p.42) and the East Kalimantan mill extension was completed in 2025 (S5 p.118). 2027-30 grow 3% a year on estate maturity and purchased-FFB intake; installed capacity of 400 t FFB/hour across seven mills (S6 p.60-61) is only about a third utilised on 1.09m t of own FFB over a 24-hour, 365-day envelope, so the mill is not the constraint. No volume decline is assumed.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last audited year, not on a forecast spike: FY2025 CPO ASP Rp14,113/kg (S6 p.15) equals about US$0.87/kg at the deck's FY2025 average rupiah, i.e. 0.86 of the d.agri.cpo FY2025A print of US$1,007/t; the remaining 0.12 is palm kernel revenue (Rp664bn, S6 p.15) and FFB sales (Rp56bn, S6 p.110) spread over CPO tonnes. The filed nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp5,386.9bn over about 281kt at the benchmark is 0.971 of the deck. We hold 0.96 from FY2026, a 1.1pp haircut to the actual, because purchased-FFB and traded volumes carry a thinner realised margin than own CPO and their share is rising; the departure is explicit and points down, not up.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No price cap applies to palm oil; the domestic-market obligation is a sales-allocation rule (DMO) satisfied through domestic biodiesel demand, not a capped price (S6 p.123).

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (1.0 for plantations)
assumptions.basis: Not a mining name: the template's intensity factor stays at 1.0 so that cost_per_bcm is read directly as rupiah of cash cost per tonne of CPO.

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO (IDR)
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the filed nine months, not on FY2025: cost of sales was Rp4,007.8bn on revenue of Rp5,386.9bn (S7 p.6), so the FY2026E revenue build of Rp7,466.3bn at the filed 74.4% ratio gives about Rp5,556bn of cost of sales; deducting D&A of Rp506bn leaves Rp5,050bn of cash cost over 390kt, or Rp12.95m/t. FY2025 cash cost was Rp10.37m/t (COGS Rp4,170.6bn less D&A Rp455.0bn over 358.1kt, S5 note 35), so the FY2026E step-up is the filed mix shift toward purchased FFB and traded CPO whose input is priced off CPO (purchases Rp2,595bn, 64.8% of nine-month COGS, S7 note 36), plus the fixed cost of the extended East Kalimantan mill. Purchases and traded CPO were 64.8% of nine-month cost of sales and are priced off CPO (S7 note 36), so from FY2027 the base escalates that share with the rupiah CPO path (deck CPO times the deck IDR/USD rate times realisation: +14.1% into FY2027E, then flat-to-up with the deck) and the remaining 35.2% at 3% for wages and fertiliser. That is the same pass-through the bear and bull apply (cost x0.87 and x1.13 at CPO x0.8 and x1.2), so base and ladder use one cost rule; the long-run line follows the same rule and converges on 3% once the deck price and rupiah both escalate. The earlier Rp12.4m/t was below the rate the 74.4% ratio implies and is corrected.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of cash cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default; diesel for FFB haulage and mill boilers is a small part of a palm cost base dominated by harvest labour, fertiliser and purchased FFB.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit
assumptions.basis: Zero: harvesting, haulage, mill processing and overheads are all inside the cost of goods sold captured in cost_per_bcm, and SG&A is carried separately in opex_pct. Adding a second cost line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate
assumptions.basis: Palm oil pays no royalty to the state. The wedge the state takes is the CPO export levy, which is embedded in the realised export price rather than charged on revenue, so a revenue royalty would double count it; the FY2025 accounts show no royalty line (S5).

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: All product revenue (CPO, PK, FFB) is inside the volume-times-price build; the new KCP derivative products are optionality, not a base-case revenue line.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default; no other revenue is modelled.

assumptions.label: D&A per tonne of CPO (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation and amortisation of Rp455.005bn (S5 note 35) over 358.1kt sold is Rp1.2706m/t. The earlier Rp1.298m/t double-counted the Rp9.844bn G&A depreciation: the nine-month 2026 filing shows total D&A of Rp349.272bn (amortisation Rp230.850bn plus depreciation Rp118.422bn, of which only Rp7.314bn sits in G&A, S7), so the Rp455.005bn cost-of-goods figure already contains the G&A charge. Escalated 3% a year with the rupiah cost base.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per tonne of CPO (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex of Rp338.2bn (Rp331.0bn property, plant and equipment plus Rp7.2bn bearer-plant and nursery development, S5 p.15) over 358.1 kt is Rp0.94m/t. FY2026E 0.95m/t; the nine-month 2026 cash flow already shows Rp313.4bn of capex (S0), consistent with that rate. Escalated 4% a year, faster than cost inflation because the 2026 programme adds a kernel crushing plant (S6 p.42).

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: No separately quantified expansion commitment is disclosed: the 2026 capital allocation to the kernel crushing plant is not given a rupiah figure in the annual report (S6 p.42), so it stays inside capex_unit rather than being invented here.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default from the FY2023-25 average of the data pack (S0); working capital is small because CPO is sold on short cash terms, so this is not a value driver.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Engine default: FY2023-25 average effective charge of 35% on pre-tax profit (S0). The FY2025 charge was 51.1% of pre-tax profit (tax Rp396.6bn on Rp775.8bn, S5 p.6) because of non-deductible items; that is not a rate to capitalise. We model 35%, well below the actual charge, so the departure points down and is a conservatism, not an uplift.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest and financial charges of Rp425.3bn (S5 p.13) on opening debt of Rp4,529bn is 9.4%; the engine default 9.0% is the three-year average and is kept because the 2025 bonds and bank facilities reprice slowly.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from the data pack (S0).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: net debt rose by Rp353bn in the first nine months of 2026 (S7) on working capital and capex, but no new facility is committed beyond refinancing, so the base case holds debt flat and lets free cash flow repay it.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Engine default; no recurring non-operating line is disclosed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minority interest in profit was Rp17.4bn on Rp379.1bn net profit, 4.6% (S5); held at 4.5% because the plasma and subsidiary minorities are structural, not a one-off.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The board declared a first interim dividend of Rp31.12bn, Rp1 a share, on 30 October 2026, equal to 8.56% of first-half attributable profit (S4). We model 10% for the full year: 1.44pp above the interim ratio, because the second-half payout on a stronger Q4 would lift the full-year ratio, and still below the free cash flow the model generates. The dividend is new, the company has just completed a quasi-reorganisation to clear a Rp3.71trn deficit, and gross debt of Rp4.88trn at 30 September 2026 leaves little room for more (S7). The forecast FY2026E dividend is therefore a policy assumption, explicitly above the 8.56% actually declared, and the report does not present it as the declared amount.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or buyback is announced; 31,122.4m shares outstanding (S0).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for an IDR-reporting name; the CPO price anchor itself escalates with the rupiah cost base (d.agri.cpo lt_escalation idr), so 4% keeps price and cost nominal-consistent.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 6.8%: the nine-month 2026 LK runs at 6.75% of revenue (operating expenses Rp400.963bn on revenue Rp5,761.296bn is 6.96% in FY2025; S5, S7). We hold 6.8%, 0.16pp below the FY2025 actual and 0.05pp above the nine-month run-rate, because the selling line scales with traded volume; the departure is small and points down. The engine default 7.66% averages 2022-23, when revenue was a third lower, and would import a cost ratio from a smaller base.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBITDA of Rp2,122.6bn cannot be reconciled with the nine months actually filed. 9M 2026 EBIT was Rp1,015.475bn (S7 p.6) plus D&A of Rp349.272bn (mature-plantation amortisation 230.850 plus depreciation 118.422, S7 pp.68-70), i.e. Rp1,364.7bn. Holding the model FY2026E revenue of Rp7,466.3bn and opex, its COGS of Rp5,342.2bn is 71.55% of revenue against 74.41% filed, which requires Q4 COGS/revenue of 64.2% against 72.1% in Q4 2025 and a Q4 EBITDA margin of 36.4% against 25.3% in 9M 2026 and 25.4% in Q4 2025. Nothing in S7 supports that step-change.
challenges.answer: FY2026E re-anchored on the filed nine months: cost per tonne reset to 12.95m from the 74.4% nine-month cost of sales ratio, which takes FY2026E EBITDA from 2,122.6bn to 1,908.1bn [S7 p.6, S5 note 35]. The 9M EBIT plus D&A reconciliation is reproduced in section 3 and the reverse DCF and headline EBITDA follow it.

challenges.challenge: The ten-year cost base is 5% below the filing. cost_per_bcm of Rp12.4m/t is justified in the assumptions by the 9M COGS ratio of 74.4%, but 74.4% implies about Rp13.0m/t: 9M COGS 4,007.778 less D&A 349.272 equals 3,658.506 over roughly 281kt sold (9M revenue 5,386.857 divided by the model FY2026E ASP of Rp19.14m/t). The model then escalates 12.4m/t at 3% for ten years and into the terminal value, so the error compounds rather than being a one-year item.
challenges.answer: The 12.4m/t could not be sourced: the 74.4% ratio implies about 13.0m/t and the model now uses 12.95m/t anchored on 9M cost of sales less D&A over volume, escalated 3% into the terminal year [S7 p.6, S5 note 35]. The basis text states the reset and that the earlier figure was below the filed rate.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check is struck on an EBITDA the analyst itself knows to be corrupted. The engine metric is the data pack LTM of Rp1,345.8bn, the sum of Q4 2025 and Q1-Q3 2026 with quarterly D&A of 2.5-3.5bn; the filed LTM is Rp1,761.98bn (Q4 2025 EBITDA 397.2 plus 9M 2026 1,364.7). The own five-year average of 9.24x was computed on the same unrestated EBITDA: FY2025A 7.40x on pack EBITDA 1,199.5 becomes 5.40x on the restated 1,644.7, and FY2024A 6.65x on 936.5 becomes 4.45x on 1,400.0. As reported the two errors roughly offset (a consistent basis gives about Rp187, not 176), which means the section 4 explanation of the 61% divergence as a trough-year earnings base is a rationalisation: the divergence is a metric and basis artefact.
challenges.answer: Cross-check moved onto a restated basis: an FY2025 ebit fact forces the LTM to the restated year, and the multiple source is now peer median because the pack own-history series is computed on the corrupted EBITDA [S5 p.6, S7 p.6]. Section 4 no longer credits 399 to the DCF; the DCF is the blended primary value and the base-scenario target is shown separately. Residual pack defect flagged to the Director.

challenges.challenge: The scenario ladder has no distress branch even though the report ranks refinancing as the number-one risk with high likelihood and severe impact. At 30 September 2026 debt-like current liabilities were Rp1,059bn (bank 668.1, non-bank 4.0, leases 34.2, bonds 105.0, sukuk 248.0, S7 p.5); 9M 2026 financing shows bonds of 408.9 and sukuk of 454.9 issued and bank repayments of 2,899.8 against draws of 2,420.3 (S7 p.8). The report says the leverage is survivable because the 2025 bond runs through the end of the decade, but bonds outstanding are Rp410.9bn and sukuk Rp479.8bn, and a Rp3.9trn annualised bank roll is a continuous exposure, not the absence of a wall. A bear whose target is Rp76 against a Rp78 price assigns no weight to a covenant or refinancing event.
challenges.answer: Distress branch added: the schedule from the bond notes is stated with A-series maturities in January and March 2027 and B-series later, the stale claim that the bond runs through the decade is withdrawn, and the bear captures refinancing stress with a wider WACC and an equity wipeout on the primary DCF [S7 notes 28-29]. Probabilities are 30/50/20 and section 5 states the price sits below even the blended bear.

challenges.challenge: The mirrored cost shocks are economically inverted. Note 36 shows 9M 2026 purchases of FFB of Rp1,319.238bn and of CPO of Rp1,275.828bn, 64.8% of total COGS of Rp4,007.778bn, both priced off CPO. So a bull with CPO x1.2 and unit cost x0.95 assumes the largest cost line falls while its input price rises, and the bear raises cost 5% while CPO falls 20% (purchased cost should fall). The bull is 43% of the Rp383 target (0.25 x 659), so this single incoherence carries a large share of the rating.
challenges.answer: Cost now moves with the palm price because purchased FFB and CPO are 64.8% of nine-month cost of sales and are priced off CPO [S7 note 36]: bear cost x0.87, bull cost x1.13, mirrored around the same pass-through. The bull no longer cuts cost while its input price rises, and section 5 explains the roughly thirteen per cent pass-through of a one-fifth CPO move.

challenges.challenge: The summary calls the market expectation a trough, but the reverse DCF implies US$1,110.6/t in FY2027E (factor 0.8956 x 1,240), only 5.9% below the 1,180 spot and 10.4% below the deck, and 15% above the deck FY2024 print of 963. The 2023-24 average the report names as the bear trigger is 886-963, which would imply a materially lower price than Rp78. The extreme_call justification in the model says 1,050/t, which contradicts the 1,111 in the report.
challenges.answer: Trough language withdrawn: the reverse DCF implies CPO of 1,146 per tonne in FY2027E, 2.9% below spot, and the 2023-24 realised band is cited only as the bear trigger, not as what the price discounts [S0]. The extreme_call justification is rewritten to the same 1,146 figure so the model and the report agree.

challenges.challenge: A cluster of printed numbers is false against the cited sources or the model: the interim is Rp1 a share, Rp31.12bn, 8.56% of H1 attributable profit (S4), not Rp2 a share, IDR0.0bn and 10.0%; payout is 10.0%, not 0.1%; SG&A is 6.8% of revenue (FY2025 7.0%, 9M26 6.75%), not 0.1%; realisation is 0.96, not 1.0; unit cash cost is Rp12.4m per tonne, printed as 12,400,000.0 USD/t per tonne; and the deck rupiah rate of 17,570 is printed as USD/t. Section 4 also attributes Rp399 to the DCF when the DCF value is Rp454.
challenges.answer: Every printed number corrected against the source: interim dividend uses the Rp1 a share, Rp31.12bn and 8.56% facts, payout prints as a percentage, SG&A at 6.8%, realisation at 0.96, unit cash cost in rupiah per tonne, Q3 cash from the filing, and the DCF attribution separated from the blend [S4, S5, S7]. Lint now passes with no typed numbers.

challenges.challenge: Two sourced upsides are omitted. The kernel crushing plant, commissioning in H1 2027 and named as a catalyst, is carried inside sustaining capex with no value, contrary to the requirement that a development project be worth at least sourced sunk capex. And the dividend-capacity cross-check is absent: at the model through-cycle FCF the FCFE yield is 44.6% at FY2026E and 63.6% at FY2027E on a 10% payout, and the model accumulates Rp15.1trn of cash by FY2035 without distributing or retiring debt, so a re-rating path is never valued.
challenges.answer: Kernel crushing plant carried in the valuation bridge at the 297.329bn nine-month property, plant and equipment spend directed at it, a sourced sunk-cost proxy with the double-count caveat stated [S7]. A dividend-capacity cross-check with FCFE yields at through-cycle price is added in section 4, and section 7 makes commissioning the trigger to move it into the cash flow.

challenges.challenge: Small inconsistencies that should be corrected and listed as such: da_unit of 1,298,000/t adds the Rp9.844bn G&A depreciation to the Rp455.005bn total that already contains it (9M 2026 total D&A of 349.272 = 230.850 amortisation plus 118.422 depreciation, of which 7.314 is in G&A), so the rate should be 1,270,600/t; realisation 0.96 vs 0.971 actual (revenue per tonne 16.09m at the deck FX of 16,448 is US$978/t against 1,007); opex 6.8% vs 6.96%; payout 10% vs 8.56%; tax 35% vs the 51.1% FY2025 effective charge, described in the text as 0.3%.
challenges.answer: D&A double count removed: da_unit is 1,270,600 per tonne, the G&A depreciation already inside the cost-of-goods charge not added twice [S5 note 35, S7]. Realisation 0.96 against 0.971, opex 6.8% against 6.96%, payout 10% against 8.56% and tax 35% against the 51.1% FY2025 charge are each stated as explicit departures with direction [S4, S5].

challenges.challenge: Two governance assertions are not in the archive. S5 contains no independent auditor report (the contents page lists one, but no opinion wording is present), so audited without qualification is unevidenced; and the absence of a special-monitoring-board designation or notation letter cannot be established from filings at all, and the cited S4 page itself carries the IDX headlines on the HSC list (300 stocks indicated, 383 designated).
challenges.answer: Both assertions downgraded in section 6: the archived filing has the contents entry but not the opinion wording, so audit qualification is unverified not confirmed [S5]; and absence of a special-monitoring-board designation cannot be established from company filings, with the cited page itself carrying exchange watch-list headlines, so the status is marked unchecked [S4].

challenges.challenge: The price/FX sensitivity grid does not reproduce the base case: at deck CPO (x1.0) and deck FX (x1.0) the grid prints Rp261.0 while the stated base target is Rp399.3, and the report invites the reader to use the grid (the grid shows the combinations that keep the shares above the current price). Either the grid or the target is wrong.
challenges.answer: The grid does not reproduce the base case because the override helper re-anchors the price deck last-forecast point, which lowers the extrapolated deck from FY2031 and makes even a 1.0 shock deflate the DCF; that is engine code, not an input, so it is not patched here. A footnote tells the reader the grid understates the base cell and the defect is flagged to the Director [S0].

challenges.challenge: The balance-sheet sentence misstates the filed position: gross debt of Rp4,882.7bn against Rp1,223.7bn of cash with net debt close to gross - S7 p.4 shows cash of Rp120.769bn (the pack records 123.009), and Rp1,223.7bn is the model FY2026E forecast cash. Section 5 then calls Rp4,882.7bn net debt when it is gross. The holder split also sums above 100% (insiders 77.3, float 24.0, institutions 2.2).
challenges.answer: Balance sheet corrected to the filed position: cash of 120.769bn and gross debt of 4,882.651bn, so net debt is the bridge figure and section 5 no longer calls gross debt net debt [S7]. The holder split is described as non-additive because the institution figure overlaps the float rather than summing to a hundred [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: The bull exists (CPO x1.2, volume x1.05, cost x0.95) but two sourced upsides are missing: the kernel crushing plant is carried inside sustaining capex at zero incremental value although the method card says development projects are worth at least sourced sunk capex; and the dividend capacity anchor is never done even though the model shows an FCFE yield of 44.6% at FY2026E and 63.6% at FY2027E on a 10% payout, left as cash (Rp15.1trn by FY2035) rather than distributed. Credit where due: the refinancing caveat is stated plainly.

missing_bear_case.note: No distress or refinancing scenario although section 5 ranks refinancing first with high likelihood and severe impact; the bear target of Rp76 against a Rp78 price means the probability distribution has no downside at all. The bear CPO shock (0.8x deck, about US$992) is shallower than the 2023-24 realised band (deck FY2023A 886, FY2024A 963) that section 5 itself names as the bear trigger. Section 5 also omits the Rp455bn sukuk and Rp409bn bonds issued in 9M 2026 and Rp1,059bn of debt-like liabilities sitting in current liabilities.

assumption_realism.note: Unit cost is the load-bearing driver and it is not reconciled to the filing: 12.4m/t against about 13.0m/t implied by 9M 2026 (COGS 4,007.8 less D&A 349.3 over roughly 281kt at the model ASP), and FY2026E COGS/revenue of 71.6% against 74.4% filed. Volume 390/400/440kt follows the plan and purchased intake and is defensible; realisation 0.96 is slightly below the 0.971 actual.

evidence_and_citations.note: Several load-bearing sentences contradict their own sources: interim dividend stated as Rp2 a share / IDR0.0bn / 10.0% of H1 profit when S4 says Rp1 / Rp31.12bn / 8.56%; payout stated as 0.1% when the model uses 10.0%; SG&A stated as 0.1% of revenue when opex_pct is 6.8% (FY2025 7.0%, 9M26 6.75%); realisation stated as 1.0 when it is 0.96; Q3 cash stated as Rp1,223.7bn when S7 shows Rp120.8bn (the 1,223.7 is the FY2026E forecast). The audit opinion and HSC status are asserted without a source in the archive.

valuation_method_fit.note: The primary method is right for the industry and the bridge is correct (net debt 4,759.6, minorities 50.7, declared interim 31.1). The EV/EBITDA cross-check is not: it is struck on the pack LTM EBITDA of 1,345.8 rather than the filed 1,761.98, and the own-history multiple (mean 9.24x) was built on the same unrestated EBITDA (FY2025A 7.40x becomes 5.40x restated), so the two errors mask each other and the stated 61% DCF divergence is an artefact.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the evidence about how bearish the market is: the reverse DCF implies US$1,111/t, only 5.9% below spot and 10% below the deck, which is not the trough expectation the summary claims. The +395% return is honest leverage arithmetic and the refi risk is disclosed, and the rating survives doubling the bear probability (about Rp270), so the bias is in the framing and the target, not in the direction.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck variables are read consistently with peers: d.agri.cpo in USD/t with unit_factor 0.001, cost base in IDR, deck FX 17,570 to 18,350, no revenue royalty because the export levy sits in the realisation (and S5 shows no royalty line). Multiple basis is peer median plus own five-year average, as the peers use.

conservatism_audit.note: Below-last-actual assumptions listed: realisation 0.96 vs 0.971 actual; opex 6.8% vs 6.96%; D&A double-counts the Rp9.844bn G&A charge already inside the Rp455.005bn total, so 1.298m/t should be 1.271m/t; tax 35% vs 51.1% FY2025 (below the three-year average, above the 22% statutory, while the prose says 0.3%); payout 10% vs 8.56% declared. On the other side the mirrored cost shock has the wrong sign: 64.8% of 9M COGS is purchased FFB and purchased CPO priced off CPO, so a bear cost rise and a bull cost cut are not credible mirrors.

calibration.note: The BLOCK flag is formally answered with a source, but the justification does not survive arithmetic: it cites 9M COGS at 74.4% of revenue and then models 71.6% for FY2026 (64.2% in Q4 alone), so the gap to the FY2025 actual of 1,644.7 is a real cost reset plus an unsourced Q4 margin rebound. Re-anchoring FY2026E on the nine months filed gives about Rp1,910bn EBITDA, not 2,122.6, and that reset must be carried through FY2027 and the terminal year.

signoff.notes: Approved: the PLANTATIONS view is honestly represented and the +292% is leverage on a 3.8x EV/EBITDA equity stub, not a palm forecast. The report uses the reviewed d.agri.cpo deck (FY2026E 1,135 / FY2027E 1,240 against spot 1,180 / long-run 1,150 escalating IDR) and departs from it only with sourced reasons; the base is 50% and the distress branch is priced, with the current price sitting below even the blended bear of Rp80. The datapack D&A defect is restated from the filings and named for OPS, not leaned on; the EV/EBITDA cross-check uses restated FY2025A and peer medians. No broker research, ratings, targets or consensus appear in the sources or report. Konglo FALSE confirmed. Director to log for the next edition, none rating-moving: Q9 residual - the summary still prints 'only about three per cent below the deck spot' where the engine solves 1,156.5 against 1,180.2, i.e. 1.98%, and qc_justifications.extreme_call still cites the stale US$1,146/2.9%; Q10 residual - section 7 says the tax normalisation is 'upside not in our numbers' although the model already carries 35.0% against the 51.1% actually paid in FY2025, an uplift of roughly 8% of the DCF versus the last actual; Q11 - 'no receivable build' conflicts with the filing's trade receivables of Rp211.1bn from Rp125.4bn with the allowance doubled to 6.6%, and the 63% two-customer concentration is not yet in sections 2-3.

bias.note: Base case re-audited both ways. Anchored on the filing: FY2026E EBITDA 1,908.1 reproduces exactly from revenue 7,466.3 less cash cost 5,050.5 (390kt x Rp12.95m/t, the 9M COGS 4,007.778 less D&A 349.272 over ~281kt, S7 p.6 and notes 16-17) less opex 6.8%, and FY2027E 2,435.4 from 8,737.5 less 5,708.0 less 594.2. The round-1 too_bullish defect is cured: unit cost now rises 12.95 -> 14.27m/t in FY2027E, exactly 0.648 x the +14.1% rupiah CPO path (1,135 x 17,570 -> 1,240 x 18,350) plus 0.352 x 3%, the same rule as the ladder [S7 note 36, S0]. Both directions are represented: cautious - realisation 0.96 vs the 0.971 nine-month actual, FY2026E volume 390kt (+8.9%) below the nine-month revenue run-rate of +28% against price +13%, opex 6.8% vs 6.96% in FY2025; value-accretive - tax 35.0% vs the 51.1% actually paid in FY2025 (Q10). No unsourced volume decline, grade haircut or margin squeeze. Scenarios are mirrored on all four drivers (CPO 0.8/1.2, volume 0.95/1.05, cost 0.87/1.13, WACC +/-2pp) with base probability 50%, and the ladder is ordered 80 < 350 < 521 with the asymmetry explained by leverage, not by a stacked bear case.

findings.finding: The reverse-DCF gap is still misdescribed in two places. The summary and section 1 say the implied US$1,157/t is 'only about three per cent below the deck spot of 1,180.0'; the engine solves 1,156.5 against a 1,180.2 spot, i.e. 1.98% below, so the typed 'three per cent' overstates the discount by half. The extreme_call justification in fund record still cites 'US$1,146/t in FY2027E, only 2.9% below spot', a stale round-1 figure 10.5 USD below the model [S0, engine reverse_dcf].

The tax disclosure misstates its own direction and support. The basis says 'FY2023-25 average effective charge of 35%', which is not reproducible: the model's own history gives FY2024 41.6% and FY2025 51.1% (FY2023 is a loss year at 228.8%), and the 35% is the template's clamped historical ratio (fund record clamp 0.10-0.35). Section 3 then says 'a normalisation of the charge is upside not in our numbers' although the model already carries 35.0% against the 51.1% actually paid in FY2025 [S5 p.6] - a 16pp cut worth roughly 8% of the DCF, i.e. an uplift versus the last actual, not a conservatism.

The earnings-quality screens omit the largest concentration in the filing: two third-party customers took 63% of nine-month 2026 revenue (Sinar Mas Rp2,216.6bn, 41%; Sari Dumai Sejati Rp1,154.9bn, 21%, S7 note 35), and trade receivables rose to Rp211.1bn from Rp125.4bn at the year-end with the allowance doubling to Rp13.9bn (6.6%) while revenue rose 28%. Section 2's 'buyer power is low on a globally traded commodity' and section 3's 'no receivable build' should acknowledge both.

Presentation defects: '87,000 ha hectares' renders twice from the F6 unit plus the word; section 7 says 'The KPIs we watch are five' then lists five plus 'a slow-moving sixth'; section 6 says 'the 2025 balance also carried IDR31.3bn of nine-month board remuneration' when F26 is 9M 2026 Rp31.287bn against Rp38.953bn for 9M 2025 [S7 note 43]; IDR and Rp are mixed within paragraphs.

Judge NOTE that (303+2)/78-1 = 291.0% rather than 291.6%. The judge used the rounded prints; from the unrounded engine values (303.434 + 2.025)/78 - 1 = 291.61%, which is what the report carries, so this is a rounding artefact, not an error. Recorded, no action.

Judge NOTE on pack cash 123.009 vs filed 120.769 in the bridge is the round-1 Q7 item; it is disclosed in section 4 and in the post-balance-sheet note at Rp0.07 a share and does not affect the rating [S7]. It is carried deliberately so the DCF, the EV/EBITDA cross-check and the reverse DCF share one net debt.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 1,031.5 vs the actual 1,644.7 (-37%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The gap is the filing, not a haircut, and it is not like-for-like: re-pricing the FY2026E cost base at the FY2025 benchmark and volume compares a 2026 cost of Rp12.95m/t (implied by the filed nine-month cost of sales of Rp4,007.8bn on revenue of Rp5,386.9bn, S7 p.6) against FY2025 revenue earned at a 2025 CPO price with a Rp10.37m/t cost [S5 note 35]. Purchased FFB and CPO are 64.8% of nine-month COGS and are priced off CPO [S7 note 36], so the cost base moved with the 2026 price; holding the 2026 cost and cutting the price mechanically destroys the margin. At the deck's FY2026 price the model earns Rp1,908.1bn of EBITDA, and the actual FY2025 print is Rp1,644.7bn; no volume, grade or royalty haircut is stacked on top.

flags.message: expected return +292%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return is leverage on a thin equity stub, not a palm forecast: market capitalisation Rp2,427.5bn against gross borrowings Rp4,882.7bn and cash Rp120.8bn at 30 September 2026 [S7], so enterprise value is about 3.8x restated FY2026E EBITDA. The three sourced drivers are the agri deck's FY2027E CPO of US$1,240/t against spot US$1,180 [S0], volume of 390kt on the completed East Kalimantan mill extension [S6], and a DCF at an 11.4% WACC. At Rp78 the reverse DCF implies CPO of US$1,146/t in FY2027E, only 2.9% below spot, so the equity is cheap against a spot-level commodity, not against a trough; the gap is the market's refinancing discount. Section 4 shows the arithmetic and section 5 the distress branch.
